content: 1. Antiretroviral therapy (ART) should be initiated as soon as possible within eight weeks of starting tuberculosis (TB) treatment. In 2012, the World Health Organization (WHO) recommended starting ART within two weeks for individuals with a CD4 count ≤ 50 cells/mm³. 2. Since 2021, WHO has recommended initiating ART within two weeks of starting TB treatment for people with drug-susceptible TB, regardless of CD4 cell count, provided TB meningitis is excluded. 3. A systematic review and meta-analysis of nine trials comparing early versus delayed ART initiation in people with HIV and TB showed a reduction in mortality with earlier ART initiation. This translates to one fewer death per 100 people, with a range of six fewer to four more deaths per 100 people. 4. In individuals with a CD4 count ≤ 50 cells/mm³, low-certainty evidence suggested no significant difference in mortality when ART was initiated within two weeks versus between two and eight weeks of TB treatment. Among those with a CD4 count > 50 cells/mm³, mortality rates were also similar between early and delayed ART initiation. 5. Low-certainty evidence indicated that AIDS-defining events were comparable between ART initiation within two weeks and between two to eight weeks of TB treatment. Similarly, viral load suppression rates did not differ significantly between these groups. 6. Very low-certainty evidence suggested an increased incidence of immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) events with ART initiation within two weeks of TB treatment compared to later initiation. However, IRIS-related mortality was uncommon. 7. Based on a public health approach, WHO now recommends starting ART within two weeks of TB treatment initiation for all people with HIV and drug-susceptible TB, regardless of CD4 count. For individuals with TB meningitis, ART should be delayed by at least four weeks due to safety concerns. 8. Concerns about increased IRIS risk with dolutegravir (DTG)-based regimens were not supported by the INSPIRING trial, which found similar IRIS incidence between DTG and efavirenz arms. These findings align with a 2019 network meta-analysis. 9. The REALITY trial, which included people with advanced HIV disease, found no increased IRIS incidence with raltegravir as an additional option. Close monitoring for IRIS and other clinical events is advised, especially for children and pregnant or breastfeeding women. 10. HIV programs should establish mechanisms for adequate monitoring, including pharmacovigilance and surveillance for drug-drug interactions. Pregnant and breastfeeding women were not included in the reviewed studies, but earlier ART initiation is unlikely to increase harm in this population and has clear benefits for maternal and child health. 11. Evidence on ART timing for individuals with drug-resistant TB and those on secondor third-line ART regimens is limited. Observational studies suggest that ART use in drug-resistant TB is associated with lower mortality and higher cure rates, but evidence quality is low to very low. 12. Co-trimoxazole prophylaxis, a combination of sulfamethoxazole and trimethoprim, should be provided to people living with HIV and TB regardless of CD4 count. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) have shown reduced mortality and morbidity with co-trimoxazole, even in areas with high antibiotic resistance. 13. Coordination between TB and HIV programs is essential to deliver uninterrupted care, reduce costs, and improve outcomes. Community engagement, patient education, and peer support are critical for adherence to co-treatment and continuation of ART after TB treatment completion. 14. A systematic review of ART delivery in TB treatment settings found increased ART uptake and timeliness, though mortality and TB treatment success data were inconsistent. Studies on TB treatment in HIV care settings showed mixed results on mortality but comparable ART uptake and TB treatment success rates. 15. Comprehensive HIV prevention strategies should be implemented for people attending TB care, including access to voluntary and confidential HIV testing, harm reduction services, and prevention of vertical HIV transmission in pregnant women. 16. WHO emphasizes the importance of monitoring and evaluation to assess the quality and effectiveness of collaborative TB/HIV activities. Standardized indicators and operational research are critical for program management and continuous improvement. 17. Antiretroviral drugs play a key role in HIV prevention. People with undetectable viral loads who adhere to ART have zero risk of transmitting HIV to sexual partners. ART during pregnancy and breastfeeding effectively prevents mother-to-child transmission. 18. Biomedical measures to prevent HIV transmission include condoms, voluntary medical male circumcision, and harm reduction services for people who inject drugs. Behavioral and structural interventions are also essential to address stigma, discrimination, and other barriers to care. 19. Healthcare settings must implement primary prevention measures, such as standard precautions and safe waste disposal, to prevent HIV transmission. Secondary prevention measures, like post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP), should also be available. 20. WHO identifies key populations at higher risk of HIV acquisition, including men who have sex with men, sex workers, people in prisons, people who inject drugs, and transgender individuals. These populations often face elevated TB risk as well. 21. Collaborative TB/HIV services should adopt a person-centered approach to maximize access and adherence, particularly for vulnerable populations.
